[[2]]

events.content: NVIDIA Data Center segment definition fiscal 2027 press release

NVIDIA’s FY2027 earnings releases define **Data Center** as one of its two market platforms, alongside **Edge Computing**. [[1]] 

Within Data Center, NVIDIA reports two sub-markets: **Hyperscale** and **ACIE**—AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise. [[1]]

**Hyperscale** comprises revenue from public-cloud providers and the world’s largest consumer-internet companies, while **ACIE** covers NVIDIA’s opportunity in diverse AI-purpose-built data centers and AI factories across industries and countries. [[1]] 

For context, NVIDIA reported Data Center revenue of **$75.2 billion in Q1 FY2027**, including **$60.4 billion** of Data Center compute revenue and **$14.8 billion** of Data Center networking revenue under its prior compute/networking presentation. [[2]]

tool_arguments.query: NVIDIA Data Center revenue Q4 FY2026 growth drivers Blackwell inference networking

events.content: NVIDIA Data Center revenue Q4 FY2026 growth drivers Blackwell inference networking

**NVIDIA Data Center revenue reached a record $62.3 billion in Q4 FY2026** (quarter ended January 2026), increasing **22% sequentially** and **75% year over year**; total company revenue was $68.1 billion. [[1]]

**The principal growth driver was the sustained ramp of Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra systems.** NVIDIA said Data Center revenue grew by roughly $11 billion versus Q3, with Blackwell architecture demand broadening across cloud providers, hyperscalers, AI-model developers, enterprises and sovereign customers. [[2]] Grace Blackwell systems represented approximately **two-thirds of quarterly Data Center revenue**, while nearly **nine gigawatts** of Blackwell infrastructure had been deployed and consumed by major cloud and hyperscale customers. [[2]]

**Inference was central to the demand thesis, rather than only training.** Management characterized agentic AI as an inflection point and positioned Grace Blackwell with NVLink as an inference platform with an order-of-magnitude lower cost per token. [[3]] NVIDIA also cited Blackwell Ultra performance of up to **50x higher** and cost up to **35x lower** for agentic AI relative to Hopper, while selected inference providers reported up to a **10x reduction in AI costs** using open-source models on Blackwell. [[3]] These economics matter because higher token throughput and lower per-token cost can improve AI-service-provider monetization and support continued infrastructure deployment. [[2]]

**Networking was the second major incremental contributor.** Q4 Data Center networking revenue was **$11 billion**, more than **3.5x** its year-earlier level. [[2]] NVIDIA attributed the year-over-year networking increase primarily to **NVLink 72 scale-up switches**, and its FY2026 10-K said Data Center networking revenue grew **142%** on the NVLink compute-fabric ramp for GB200 and GB300 systems plus growth in Ethernet and InfiniBand platforms. [[2]] [[4]]

**Bottom line:** Q4 FY2026 Data Center growth reflected a platform sale—Blackwell/Blackwell Ultra compute systems, inference-driven customer ROI, and tightly coupled scale-up and scale-out networking—not simply stand-alone GPU shipments. [[4]]

tool_arguments.query: NVIDIA Data Center revenue Q2 FY2027 growth drivers Blackwell inference networking

events.content: NVIDIA Data Center revenue Q2 FY2027 growth drivers Blackwell inference networking

**Q2 FY2027 Data Center performance.** NVIDIA generated **$89.0 billion** of Data Center revenue in the quarter ended **July 26, 2026**, up **18% sequentially** and **117% year over year**; it accounted for roughly 92% of the company’s $96.2 billion total revenue. [[1]]

**Blackwell was the principal product driver.** Hyperscale revenue reached **$49 billion**, increasing **13% sequentially**, which management attributed to sustained Blackwell strength and incremental GPU capacity coming online. [[2]] NVIDIA also framed the platform upgrade as economically important: estimated content/revenue opportunity per gigawatt rose from about **$18 billion for Hopper** to **$25 billion for Grace Blackwell**, reflecting the sale of a broader system rather than GPUs alone. [[2]]

**Inference is enlarging both demand and NVIDIA’s attainable content.** Management described frontier AI labs as having extraordinary demand for both training and inference compute, with their expansion constrained principally by available compute capacity rather than end-customer demand. [[2]] NVIDIA’s strategic pitch is that its NVLink-72 rack-scale systems are “fungible” across the AI lifecycle—data preparation, pretraining, post-training, and agentic inference—rather than being optimized only for a single inference workload. [[2]] This is particularly relevant as agentic inference becomes more complex and requires scalable, multi-GPU systems, supporting demand for Blackwell-based AI factories. [[2]]

**Networking was a material complementary growth lever.** NVIDIA reported another record networking quarter, with networking revenue up **18% quarter over quarter**; Spectrum-X Ethernet grew **2.6x year over year**. [[3]] The broader full-stack offering includes GPU and CPU compute plus **NVLink scale-up networking** and **InfiniBand or Ethernet scale-out networking**, enabling NVIDIA to capture networking content alongside accelerator deployments. [[2]]

**Demand breadth supported the result.** Data Center growth came from both hyperscale customers and the ACIE group—AI cloud/neocloud, industrial, and enterprise customers—rather than relying solely on hyperscalers. [[2]] NVIDIA also cited a global AI-infrastructure buildout across hyperscalers, AI labs, AI-native firms, enterprises, and sovereign customers; it noted cloud-industry backlog above **$2 trillion** and anticipated top-five hyperscaler capex of nearly **$800 billion in 2026** and **$1.3 trillion in 2027**. [[2]]

private_messages.content:
**Q2 FY2027 Data Center performance.** NVIDIA generated **$89.0 billion** of Data Center revenue in the quarter ended **July 26, 2026**, up **18% sequentially** and **117% year over year**; it accounted for roughly 92% of the company’s $96.2 billion total revenue. [[1]]

**Blackwell was the principal product driver.** Hyperscale revenue reached **$49 billion**, increasing **13% sequentially**, which management attributed to sustained Blackwell strength and incremental GPU capacity coming online. [[2]] NVIDIA also framed the platform upgrade as economically important: estimated content/revenue opportunity per gigawatt rose from about **$18 billion for Hopper** to **$25 billion for Grace Blackwell**, reflecting the sale of a broader system rather than GPUs alone. [[2]]

**Inference is enlarging both demand and NVIDIA’s attainable content.** Management described frontier AI labs as having extraordinary demand for both training and inference compute, with their expansion constrained principally by available compute capacity rather than end-customer demand. [[2]] NVIDIA’s strategic pitch is that its NVLink-72 rack-scale systems are “fungible” across the AI lifecycle—data preparation, pretraining, post-training, and agentic inference—rather than being optimized only for a single inference workload. [[2]] This is particularly relevant as agentic inference becomes more complex and requires scalable, multi-GPU systems, supporting demand for Blackwell-based AI factories. [[2]]

**Networking was a material complementary growth lever.** NVIDIA reported another record networking quarter, with networking revenue up **18% quarter over quarter**; Spectrum-X Ethernet grew **2.6x year over year**. [[3]] The broader full-stack offering includes GPU and CPU compute plus **NVLink scale-up networking** and **InfiniBand or Ethernet scale-out networking**, enabling NVIDIA to capture networking content alongside accelerator deployments. [[2]]

**Demand breadth supported the result.** Data Center growth came from both hyperscale customers and the ACIE group—AI cloud/neocloud, industrial, and enterprise customers—rather than relying solely on hyperscalers. [[2]] NVIDIA also cited a global AI-infrastructure buildout across hyperscalers, AI labs, AI-native firms, enterprises, and sovereign customers; it noted cloud-industry backlog above **$2 trillion** and anticipated top-five hyperscaler capex of nearly **$800 billion in 2026** and **$1.3 trillion in 2027**. [[2]]

{"summary":"NVIDIA Data Center revenue (most recent periods):

- Q2 FY2027 (ended July 26, 2026): $89.0B, up 117% YoY and 18% sequentially. Major drivers: Blackwell/GB300 system ramp (Hyperscale $49B, +13% seq); inference demand expanding as Blackwell systems are "fungible" across training/inference; networking up 18% QoQ, Spectrum-X Ethernet 2.6x YoY. (S1.1, S9.1-S9.3)
- Q1 FY2027 (ended April 26, 2026): $75.2B, up 92% YoY and 21% sequentially. Principal driver: Blackwell/GB300 ramp, especially GB300 NVL72; inference demand inflection; networking up 199% YoY; Hyperscale $38B, ACIE $37B (+31% seq). (S3.1-S3.3)
- Q4 FY2026 (ended Jan 2026): $62.3B, up 75% YoY and 22% sequentially. Blackwell/Blackwell Ultra systems (~2/3 of revenue); inference central to demand thesis; networking $11B, >3.5x YoY growth. (S7.1-S7.4)

NVIDIA defines its Data Center segment as one of two market platforms (with Edge Computing), comprising Hyperscale (public-cloud / largest internet companies) and ACIE (AI clouds, industrial, enterprise). Within Data Center, revenue splits into compute ($60.4B in Q1 FY2027, $60.4B implied in Q2) and networking ($14.8B in Q1, up 18% QoQ in Q2)."}
